utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Perhaps we first resume the examination of the witness Commander Kolp and then deal with other issues still outstanding. Mr. Usher would you please bring in Mr. Kolp. [The witness entered court

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Commander Kolp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, I have a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first try to make my computer run. Yes. It is now connected. Commander Kolp, you told us yesterday about complaints you made about sniping incidents to Major Indjic. Could you please tell us in more detail what his responses were to these complaints.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What Major Indjic usually answered, it was never a precise answer. He would say "Yes, we will see about it." And he said that their snipers are firing on us and he also often replied to me sometimes. Sometimes he would say, "This is not very serious, only a few shots," and that he would see what he could do. That was that. I have to say that when I met him, it was mostly in the afternoon to speak of this subject and I have to say that he was mostly intoxicated or at least influenced by drink and, therefore, what he said wasn't very coherent. Generally, as a rule, he never took my request seriously except on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... any denial of sniping activities from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This happened. It occurred that Major Indjic would say, "Yes, I think you are exaggerating, nothing is going on. This is not a few shots that will make a great deal of difference." That was his usual answer, as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday about the impression you had about the authority of Major Indjic. Could you give us facts on which this impression was based.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes certainly. The only point of contact which was authorised and it is important to say and I will try and speak in some order. In the PTT building which is the HQ of the Sarajevo Sector there were three offices for liaison, for the three warring parties. So there was a Bosnian Muslim office -- liaison office, then there was a Bosnian Croat liaison office and then a Bosnian Serb liaison office. My first task is these people were there since I was a liaison officer authorised and I had a UN ID card. So when there was the slightest problem, I would first go to see them. It was simple. I would just go downstairs one floor, without any danger, I would be facing them and I would be able to explain the problem. As far as the Bosnian Serbs were concerned, I would discuss with -- the problem with them and I would never obtain an answer, because in fact, the answer would be, "we have to contact Lukavica and we have to contact Major Indjic in Lukavica." So it was Major Indjic. At a given point, since there were no results after a very short period of time I had the opportunity to go myself and I practically went every day from then on. I went to Lukavica to negotiate with Major Indjic. Major Indjic would receive visitors in his office in Lukavica and he would receive all kinds of people. This is where I saw the UNMOs, the United Nations monitors, and they would go directly to see him there. Then I saw members of international organisations, who, when they had problems, they would go to him and did not want to sort it out with the UN militaries who were present there, so they would go directly to him. And then, as I said yesterday, I also saw the Serbian militaries which is normal, since this was a Serbian HQ, but also the paramilitaries who would go there. And as I was passing through the Serbian checkpoint, the Sierra 1 Kobiljaca and the Sierra 4 at the Kasindolska airport and so on, the police would never take any decision. They would never dare take any decisions, that was my impression. They would have to report to Major Indjic. They had to report to the military branch. The militaries had the power. I wouldn't really like to say that, but they had the -- anything that was to do with operations. It was the military who decided. So it went to Major Indjic. Everything was reported to him. So when I was called to see a certain Zoravko Zgonjanin , who was a Colonel, he was the head of police in Ilidza, the same thing happened, I had a long meeting with him and he never wanted to say yes or no. He said, "I have to contact my superiors and he said to me who these were." This was in Lukavica and the person was Major Indjic. As for me, in my opinion, this was a key person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever make any observations on whether Major Indjic would then decide by himself or would he report to the next higher level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot but tell you what is my opinion, and in fact, I never asked Major Indjic the question, "Are you going to talk to the general or not? Are you going to talk to the colonel at the main staff." I never directly asked him the question. As for me, my impression was that -- was that Major Indjic decided by himself on a number of issues, but he did not decide on everything. And the reason why he didn't decide on everything, again, I had the occasion, or a minor experience, I had there, and that of my predecessors, we attended there and we also had to read reports. But in any case the commander in chief had to, if not take decisions, then at least would say "okay, you did well, or do nothing." But he would have to be informed of a number of things. The commander in chief of any unit would have to know what is going on. It is true that he cannot know everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question concerns the efforts you made to put containers into position in order to protect civilians, as far as I understand. You said that when it was tried to put these containers into position that those who did try, were fired at. Did I understand you well when you intended -- that you intended to say that they are fired at by snipers or by any other weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this happened indeed. It was -- we were requested to do this and Major Indjic agreed. This was the Sector Sarajevo command and it was a higher rank -- higher level of command than mine and also higher than Major Indjic's. So this was an operation that was prepared by the Sarajevo Sector. It was prepared by the HQ of the Sarajevo Sector, its commander and by a specialised branch called the G-5 and this is a military branch which takes care of the relations with humanitarian organisations that can bring assistance to the civilians and the civilian life. So the decision was taken after several rounds of negotiations at which I did not -- I did not attend in Sarajevo Sector and Lukavica in order to place these containers, in order to protect, of course, but also to protect the tram-line since the tram, although it was on and off running, but like Sarajevo it was itself a symbol and the UNPROFOR wanted to have this tram running and to bring a little bit of happiness to these people. But for the Serbs, this was considered that this was a symbol that they did not wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sniping that was fired at those who tried to put into position the containers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were probably snipers but shots were considerable more than just two or three of snipers. There was also RPG-7 that was fired. So this was again another level when we would compare it to the snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever experience when you were located in the PTT building any presence of ABiH military equipment in or around the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the building, no. Around the building, it is possible. I believe that they had a kind of a bus which they made armoured and they moved it every now and then and it is possible. As I said, there were provocations and I have seen on a couple of occasions that this armoured bus which had military colours and with a BH sign on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How were those in the PTT building respond to that provocation, if it was a provocation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when -- as a serious provocation, for it to be a serious provocation, the chief of operations of the Sarajevo Sector would send one of his officers to the liaison office, the Bosniak liaison office, which was in the PTT building or I would go myself. I went on several occasions for various things. But this is how it happened. And in general, what we could call a provocation, it was never very long. But it is true that it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My last question to you is about what you told us yesterday on the possibility of firing from within the ABiH territory, if I may say so, to targets within that same territory. Did you ever observe or did you ever gain any knowledge on snipers shooting from within the ABiH controlled area targeting civilians within that same area? A Mr. President, as far as I know, no. I cannot say that this is so. I would say that everything is possible. It is probable that myself, as I told you, if there was a provocation, and I would be in a situation like that. But, I was never present when something like that occurred. And I never heard that specifically this could have taken place. There were rumours that said that this was possible, but I would say that I was never implicated in the operational branch of the Sarajevo Sector where they received proper information. As you know, every nation, a little bit work for themselves. So they kept certain things to themselves. So, as far as I know, no, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not what we usually do, as you know, Mr. Mundis. Since yesterday you had no further questions, but if you keep the clock in the back of your mind, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp in response to a question by Judge El Mahdi you expressed that paramilitaries were controlled by difficulty on the Bosnian Serb side and that they did not differentiate between civilians and military when engaging the enemy. You also said you were never in contact with these paramilitaries apart from seeing them in the Lukavica headquarters on a few occasions. And my question is, did you ever see these paramilitary forces at any other time or place, other than in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes it occurred, although it was from afar, because I was blocked for several days. It happened that I saw these kind of people in the area of Hadzici, which is the road which goes from Sarajevo on to Blazuj and then there is the road to Pale, Konjic, Split. But the area of Hadzici is where the road where the convoys are trying to pass would regularly get blocked. And on a couple of occasions, I saw them there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the shelling of the library that you testified about yesterday, do you know when that shelling occurred? What time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't tell you at all. Although, I could tell you that this happened before I arrived in Sarajevo. So this must have happened in 1992, perhaps beginning of 1993, but this happened before I arrived in Sarajevo. What I saw was a programme on it as everything was reported what happened. So this was a propaganda to me, but this was before I arrived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And finally Commander Kolp, in response to a question from the Presiding Judge, you testified that Major Indjic would take some decisions on his own, in your opinion. Can you elaborate and tell us what type of decisions Major Indjic would take by himself without necessarily referring to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can without any problems confirm that as far as the clearances, the authorisations of passage are concerned, for most convoys, the typical type of convoys, Major Indjic would take decisions. But I can also say that when more important things were involved also convoys, but humanitarian convoys of a certain so-called sensitive material in the eyes of the Bosnian Serbs this automatically had to be transmitted to Pale. So Pale was the main staff HQ of the Bosnian Serb army. In fact it was in Han Pijesak. But Pale was where the decisions were taken. So this was the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you Commander Kolp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this cause the Defence to put additional questions as well? May I then ask you to keep the clock in the back of your mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp we spoke about Major Indjic. When asked by my learned colleague you said that he issued permits and had contact with the headquarters. Can you tell us in which capacity Major Indjic was in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean "in which capacity he was in Lukavica"? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were his responsibilities? Do you know anything about that? You said that you yourself were a liaison officer. Can you tell us what were Major Indjic's responsibilities? What was his post, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what I know and what I discovered for myself. Although I was absolutely not a part of the structure or in the hierarchical chain of Major Indjic, so I don't know what his job description was at the time. But I can tell you that according to the context of the head, Major Indjic was an officer who was a coordinator with a certain authority to decide, to take decisions. But, again, as you are asking me the question, knowing the structure, I believe that for more important things, as I said already in answering a question asked by the Prosecution, Major Indjic had to answer to his chief about things that he did. It is inconceivable in a military system and you probably know more about it than I do. That certainly in the Serb army or in the VRS, the army of the Bosnian Serbs is that there is a hierarchical system which is in place and this is a necessary system when one is in military. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Major Indjic was the liaison officer between UNPROFOR and Main Staff and that the Main Staff decided on humanitarian convoys and humanitarian assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is a compound question and might be confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please split it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, would you agree with me that Major Indjic was a liaison officer with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was certainly a liaison officer but an ordinary liaison officer like I was, has no power to decide and Major Indjic had apparently certain authority to decide on his level. So he was a liaison officer, but he was more than a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you basing that conclusion on the fact that Major Indjic issued permits for the passage of humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among other things, yes. But as I told you already, I don't know whether I was asked that question, but I believe that I stated this on one occasion. For one problem, I think this may have been a problem of shelling or sniping, one or the other. I saw Major Indjic and I asked him that this should calm down and after a certain time because there would have to be a way some time maybe to find the good people on the right place and this stopped. So that happened on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us which incident shelling, in which part, in which part of the town did you inform Major Indjic of? Can you be more precise, please. You said that you delivered a protest, but was this protest formulated in such a way as to include exact facts concerning this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I cannot tell you. I cannot remember the place where either the shelling or shellings have taken place. I remember I met Major Indjic to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kolp. And just one more question. You spoke about a container that was placed in front of the building of the Oslobodjenje when you said that there was firing from Nedzarici which was controlled by the Serb forces on -- there was firing on the members of the UN. Did you inform the Serb side that containers would be place in that part of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, the containers were not placed in front of the Oslobodjenje building. They were placed between in order to cut the -- the street, the so-called --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But my question was: Did you inform the Serb side as well and did you reach an agreement with them to have the containers placed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you very simply that this was an operation for the sector which was quite complex which was organised by the Sarajevo Sector, by the UN forces, by the HQ of the Sarajevo Sector, by Major [redacted] staff. This was quite a large operation where I was support for the G-5 branch. I was there simply as an observer with Colonel Prouteau [phoen] who was a legionnaire with whom I worked and probably there had been reactions but not from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, therefore, you are telling us that you don't know whether the Serb side had been informed and whether there had been an agreement reached concerning the placement of this containers with the Serb side? I am speaking this from your point of view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No absolutely not. The Serb party, the Serb side was informed by the Sarajevo Sector that there would be containers that would be placed in this spot. And I know that, but I can't tell you who it was. It would be impossible for me to tell you. I know the response was given by the Main Staff of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I don't know who replied, but there was a response to the Sector Sarajevo -- Sarajevo Sector HQ. There was a response and it said that they would not accept the containers placed in that spot there. That is the only thing I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While you stayed in Sarajevo, can you confirm to us that in the part of the town which was controlled by the army of the Republika Srpska as well as the area that was controlled by the army of BH, that both sides at the front line had trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. There were networks of trenches, communicating corridors almost everywhere and the front line was determined and it was impossible to find out whose was whose. Whose trench belonged to whom. But there were trenches everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Commander Kolp [Interpretation], you have completed your testimony before this Chamber. Thank you, Commander Kolp, for coming here and for answering all the questions from the Prosecution and from the Defence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is with great pleasure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I do know that the interpreters might not understand any Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no documents tendered into evidence so that we don't have to give any decisions in that respect. Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I think we first have to deal with some documents in respect of the testimony of Mr. Magnusson, but I think it should be done in closed session. Could we please turn into closed session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session now, again. Before you raise an issue, Mr. Ierace, may I ask you one question. The Chamber received a submission of an expert report, I would say demographic expert report with three names on it. Is there one specific author that could take responsibility for the whole of the report because it is important for us if we have to give a decision, even after the Defence has given its opinion on it. But we would like to know whether all three authors or one of the three authors would be in a position to take full responsibility for the whole report. Because if it was just for part of the report, then we would like to know which part of the report was made under the responsibility of which author, since it might have consequences for calling witnesses to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is such a person and that is Ewa Tabeau whose name -- and indeed, I added her name to the list or at least identified the statistics expert as being Ewa Tabeau in the list which I handed up last Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You expect that she can take full responsibility for the context of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I did understand that you have another issue that you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday morning, or rather yesterday in the first session of evidence, Mr. Piletta-Zanin expressed interest in hearing from the Prosecution in relation to a particular topic. I was unable to discern what the topic was, but it seems, Mr. President, that you did. And I think you described it as a grattage. I would be grateful for some elimination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was the rubbing outs of some parts of medical reports where old dates and other information seemed to be have been removed, before new entries, visible entries were made. I think that is the issue Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to hear an answer from the -- and a possible explanation from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. I will give out an explanation to the Trial Chamber. I think that arose during the evidence of witnesses taken by Mr. Stamp. I will report back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then hear from you. If these are the issues we had to discuss at this very moment, then could the Prosecution call its next witness and that would be a witness who will testify in open court, but as soon as documents will be referred to, we have to turn into closed session because of the protective measures in respect of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Michael Carswell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you please lead the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I will withdraw from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, I take it that you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, I take it that you are English speaking. Mr. Carswell, before giving evidence in this Tribunal, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated, Mr. Carswell. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is your name Michael Kent Carswell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you born in 1945?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you retired major from the, that is, retired from the Canadian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you join the Canadian armed forces in 1963?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In 1992 were you posted to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And by then, I think you had some 30 years, 29 years experience in the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the 7th of December -- I withdraw that. On the 6th of January 1993 were you made the Deputy Senior Military Observer in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the proper terminology would be the Deputy Sector Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you stay in Sarajevo and in that position until the 20th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness please come closer to the microphone and perhaps speak a bit more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you heard the request of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could assist you in perhaps moving the microphone a bit closer to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did your duties include the compilation of what became known as "sit-reps" on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were the sit-reps, was that a shorthand term for situation report, being a report on certain classes of activity and other general observations over the previous 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: In general terms, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At that stage I think there were two sides of military observers being the Papa side and the Lima side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the Papa side refer to the Presidency side, that is the side of the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the Lima side refer to L for Lukavica being the side controlled by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were there a number of military observers on each side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As of February 1993, were there about 60 such observers?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In a total of 14 observation posts?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 11 of those being on the Serb side and 3 on the Bosnian government side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was Patrick Haneberry the Lima commander at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: He was one of two that I dealt with at that time, sir. There was another individual that preceded him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you prepare as well as the daily sit-reps, a monthly summary of events?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown Exhibit 752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a protected document, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President, and at this stage, perhaps we should go into closed session, the second portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it depends on whether it will be shown on the ELMO or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't propose to take that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that private session would have the same effect --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On reflection, I think I can avoid the need for private session in relation to that document at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is not necessary, if you don't apply for it even being aware of the protective status of the statement, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the document we shown to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document in front of you as your -- as an end of the month report for the month of January?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was this particular monthly report prepared by Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It was prepared by Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler and I. I would do the initial draft and he would read it, and it would then be forwarded it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think his name and signature appear on the last page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am afraid, Mr. Ierace, and Mr. Carswell, that you are developing a speed which might cause some difficulties for the interpreters. So if you would -- if you would look at your screen and perhaps wait to answer the question until the text stops moving, so then the text has been translated. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During the three months that you occupied that position in Sarajevo, did you on occasion travel around the territory occupied by the Bosnian Serb army in the vicinity of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How frequently would you do that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It would depend on access in that, if there was significant action on the front line, it would be difficult to get across. However, I was not restricted by either the Bosnian side or the Serb side at their checkpoints. I probably would get across, at a minimum, weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Having crossed over to the Bosnian Serb side, did you then move around to various observation posts and other parts of that territory?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to visit gun positions on the Bosnian Serb army side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How often would you do that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Initially, when I was getting acquainted with the area, in the first week, I was there in January, that was daily. After that, the teams I met on the -- on the Lima side were pretty much taking care of the close liaison with the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you visit any gun sites after that first week in January?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How often did you do that from that point until when you left on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Probably -- this is a guess, sir, but I would -- six or seven times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Over the course of those various visits, did you form any opinion, having regard to your military background, as to the professionalism or otherwise of the commanders of the gun positions on the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that impression or opinion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: My impression was -- two answers to one question. The command post staff on the gun positions, to me, were very professional and I suspect that they were ex-JNA, seemed to be very efficient. The gunners that I spoke to, the men actually servicing the guns, were probably at draftee level in their level of training. However, I would say they were quite familiar with the weapons they were using.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity with the assistance of interpreters to speak to members of the gun crews?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you form, firstly, any impression over the three months that you were in that position having access, I take it, to reports from the military observers beneath you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to form an impression from that material and your own direct observation as to whether any of the shelling fire originating from the Bosnian Serb army side towards the city of Sarajevo was other than aimed at specific targets?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I believe the targets were -- when the target list would come down to the gun position and was given to them, they were obviously specific targets. Therefore, I am not quite sure what you are leading up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I will rephrase the question in that case. Did you form any opinion as a result of your observations and exposure to the daily reports from the staff beneath you as to whether any of the shelling originating from the Bosnian Serb army side of the confrontation line targeted anything other than legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The shelling, in my impression, on occasion did target non-military targets. I would like to elaborate a bit on that, sir, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: In my perspective, a legitimate target would be a convoy or whatever moving through town, an opposition convoy. There were times when I got the impression -- I am not doing this well -- when I got the impression they were shelling in an area where somebody had been where the opposition had a position -- in a position the opposition had been but had since moved away. So the target -- I am talking myself into a corner here. The target would be less than military, sir. There could be a glimmer of hope by somebody that it could be classed as military. We are dealing with random firing into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What would you say about that, random firing into the city?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. That was not so much near military positions, in my experience. That was more so from the mortar positions which were very difficult to track.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please so down.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Which were very difficult to attack -- or to track, in that they were highly mobile. So we had difficulties keeping tabs on the positions of the 82 millimetres and the 120 millimetre, and I strongly suspect that there was random firing going on from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you understand by the term "random firing"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Not directed by the headquarters where the commander of the weapon or the group of weapons that he has might just decide at a whim to drop a few rounds in, and I am quite sure that happened on a number of occasions. And there was also -- there was also some anti-aircraft fire that would go in with air bursts and, again, that seemed quite random because that could land anywhere virtually over any building. And it was designed as anti-personnel fire, obviously, because it was about 20 metres above the ground, 30 metres above the ground, and that is roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just to divert for a minute, when you say the bursts were 20 to 30 metres above the ground, could you explain to us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The fuse can be set to explode at various heights. And these ones would probably be set at -- I'm not an anti-aircraft gunner so I'm by no means an expert, but the bullets would explode and throw the shrapnel downwards, much more effective than a round that would hit the ground and explode out. This was in a shower effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Indeed, is there something about the firing pattern of an anti-aircraft gun which makes it difficult, if not impossible, to aim it specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the interpreters have problems keeping up, and it is very difficult for me to follow due to the speed at which it is proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You get the messages from the B/C/S interpreters. I also noticed that the speed is such that all interpreters must have problems, whether they can cope with it or not. So if you would please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will rephrase that last question. Could you tell us something about the ability of an anti-aircraft gun to fire at a specific target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, I am not an anti-aircraft gun expert, but my knowledge is that they could probably pin the area down that they wanted to, they that wanted to hit, within about 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, I will take you back to the conversations that you had with gun crews or gun battery crews. As a result of those conversations, did you form any impression as to their understanding, that is the ones you spoke to, their understanding of what it was that they were hitting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The gunners in the majority of the positions, the men on the guns, were not able to see the target except in two positions, the two positions that I am aware of. So they thought, and again I am discussing it with them through the interpreter, they thought that were firing -- firing military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many members of gun crews did you speak to, approximately, over the three months that you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Probably 20 to 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it this was expressed to you in so many words by them. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As part of my job, as my job was at the time, was to get a feel for -- get a feel for both sides and what is going on and how they are doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you said that there were two exceptions to that, that is, two exceptions to their inability to sight the target. What were those two exceptions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: There were two positions, one on the south-east corner, on the high ground overlooking Sarajevo, and there was a second one on the base of the airport, that would be in the south-west side, which also looked right over the airport in the south-west of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to those conversation with the gunners, did you ever discuss with them any specific targets in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: In particular one, and that was the so-called -- sorry, the hospital. And I wanted to know whether those gunners were aware that they were firing on a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The evidence is that there were two main hospitals in Sarajevo at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Kosevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And what did you learn when you questioned them about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The gunners were young, and I believe that they were under the impression that those were military -- a legitimate military target. In all cases -- in all cases they told me that that was an army barracks, being used as an army barracks, and in some cases, I was told that the Bosnians were firing from that by mortar, from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did they tell you where they -- who had told them or how they learned that Kosevo hospital was a military barracks? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't ask them that. I didn't pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have told us that, with the exception of the two positions that had a direct view, the gunners relied on targets being given to them. Did you learn anything as to the lines of communication to the gun batteries?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was my definite impression from both discussions at Lukavica headquarters, and lesser on the gun positions, that the orders would come from Pale through to Lukavica, and then Lukavica would assign the target list to the various gun positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say that the target list would be assigned from Pale through Lukavica to the gun positions, who at the gun positions would receive that target list?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The battery command post would receive that target list. They would plot the targets, send the information to the guns, which would then fire on order of the battery headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: By the time it came to the guns, would it be a grid reference or something else as you understood it, if you knew?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I don't know. I saw them working the gun -- the command post. I saw them working on the maps, but whether they received it as a target number or a grid reference, I couldn't say, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you refer to target numbers, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: A target number, sir, is a pre-selected target which either can be -- which either can be live registered, in other words they will fire until they have the range down, or it can simply be taken off the map and the computations put in for the laying of the guns, but not fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make any observations as to the means of communication from Lukavica to the command posts of the gun batteries?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I saw two means while I was there: Land line, telephone, and some of the more important CPs had wireless radio in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "CP"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It's a command post, sir. Battery command post

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any gun positions that appeared to be without personnel?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What did you understand to be the purpose of those?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It was my impression that the Serbs were short gunners, therefore, not possible to man every gun position all day. So they moved the gunners around to fire from the various positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you have any understanding as to whether the guns had been pre-sighted or not, that is in the unmanned positions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, sir, that wouldn't -- they would get a target once they manned that position, which would be virtually anywhere. So the guns were put in position, and in some cases, covered, and in some cases, open to the elements, but awaiting the crews, simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you ever at a gun position when it was operating, that is, a gun battery?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On those occasions, did you observe the commanders to be apparently in communication using either the radio or land line or both?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Can I elaborate a bit on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I didn't see at any time the guns do any random shooting. To me -- and, of course, I wasn't in the command post all the time. To me, the target seemed to be selected, sent down to the command post again through the chain I had indicated earlier, and the gunners would then carry out their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us that your impression was that the orders originated from Pale and you said, I think, that you gained that impression in part from your visits to Lukavica. Who at Lukavica gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I spoke to the -- on my initial in clearance and familiarization, I spoke to the UNMOs that were in Lukavica, and that is what I was told. I didn't put that question directly to any of the Serb officers in Pale -- sorry in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were there occasions when you protested to Lukavica in relation to shelling activities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there a mechanism set up for you to do that, that is, when it was to be done at very short notice?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Generally, what we did, is we would get a hold of the military observers, get a hold of the military observers in Lukavica, and they would immediately go to the Serbian OPs room the Serbian OPs room, and pass on the information. If communications were out with Lukavica, we would go downstairs, talk to the Serbian LO who was working in the first floor of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just to be clear from that, I take it from that answer you were based in the PTT building in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you would speak to the LO. I take it that's the Serb liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And who did you understand the liaison officer would contact when you protested to him or her?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It would be Lukavica, and I am not exactly sure, but I suspect it would be the operations room in that most of our requests, the great majority of our requests, were transmitted very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the operations room that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The one -- I assume there were a number there. I am only aware of one and that was in the main headquarters building as you come in the gate, on the right, right beside the military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the building complex at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever meet the corps commander during your time in Sarajevo, that is the commander of the corps, the relevant corps of the Bosnian Serb army operating in that area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: General Galic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to protest to him about shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The conversation, as I recall - and it is somewhat cloudy over 10 years, 9 and-a-half - covered that area. In specific terms, what we were generally over there on the two occasions that come to mind were shelling of the UNMO positions and shelling in and around UNMO vehicles as they were moving, military observer vehicles. During the course of the conversation, it would generally be brought up about the overall shelling, but specifically, sir, I can't remember the text of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You have told us that you observed there to be random firing. Were you aware as to whether there were any civilian casualties from such random firing originating from the Bosnian Serb army controlled side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever protest to General Galic, in whatever terms, about firing, that is unlawful firing, which occasioned civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The immediate response to the shelling would be to go through our Lukavica headquarters, directly to the Serbs. That would then be brought up generally by the Lukavica military observers to the relevant commander who happened to be on the ground at that time or when they could get a hold of him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Earlier when you explained the topics covered by you when you met General Galic, you included in those, and I will now quote your words, "During the course of the conversation, it would generally be brought up about the overall shelling." Did that include the random shelling?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the response from General Galic, and I appreciate you have already pointed out it was 9 and a-half-years ago, but perhaps you could indicate was there any denial of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the nature of the response?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The nature of the response varied from individual to individual. But General Galic, I cannot be absolutely certain of his response, but it was in general terms, sir. It would have been in defence of the Serbian homeland and it is their attempt to preserve the culture. Of course, that is not the words, but that would be the general gist of the circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You mentioned that the response varied from individual to individual. How many different people -- different individuals, that is, in the Bosnian Serb military leadership did you complain to about random shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Specifically, there only would have been two that I dealt with. And that would have been the Deputy Corps Commander and then again on a few occasions the Corps Commander. The military observers would be making their reports to the Serbs on -- on what we would direct them from PTT headquarters on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the Deputy Corps Commander that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Unfortunately, sir I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On how many separate occasions did you complain to General Galic about random shelling of Sarajevo causing civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: On two occasions, sir, in the course of our discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When was the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It was early in my tour over there in February, mid to late February, I believe, and it was I think when the chief UNMO was down. I know I accompanied him at one time and it is not clear in my diary exactly what that time was. But I think it is in mid to late February and we spoke on that occasion. Albeit, I was the number two on the ground, sir. The chief military observer was running the discussion with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts did that conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: In the Lukavica headquarters, the OPs room that I had mentioned earlier, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When was the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: When we were with the sector commander. It escapes me when it was. It would be have been in March, definitely March or possibly early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: This one was before sir in the Lukavica headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I notice the time Mr. President. Would it be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this is a convenient moment we will have a break now until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Carswell, I was asking you some questions about some meetings that where you were present and also General Galic. Did you form any impression of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: My impression was that he had a very good grasp of what we were doing and what our mandate was on the UNMOs. It was both particular -- both readings were rather amicable. There was no hard feeling like that or manifested like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Rather amicable, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He listened to our complaints and in fact took action of them -- caused action to be taken actually. In general terms, sir, the -- in particular the second meeting I felt was a gain for the UNMOs and for the situation in that we voiced our concerns and probably within a day or so, they had been actioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever raise --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, I think the interpreters are still having problems because of the speed of your delivery. If you would perhaps, with the leave of the Presiding Judge, sit forward and make a conscience effort to please speak slower, it might help. Did you ever raise with General Galic the question of where his orders came from or did he ever say anything on that topic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't remember the specific conversations. I have a general knowledge of them and I don't remember that being brought up at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just a trick that might help you to slow down, if you look at the transcript on the screen in front of you, after each phrase, could you wait until the transcript has caught up before you commence the next phrase of your sentence. Do you follow what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You have told us that for immediate communication you would speak to the liaison officer downstairs in the PTT building. Do you know the form of communication that he had to the Lukavica headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I believe they had two forms of communication, sir. They used the Motorola and I think they also had land line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the operation of the gun batteries, you have said that there were some unmanned positions. Where were they in relation to the manned gun batteries? Was there any pattern to that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: My impression, sir, was that they would be -- they would be subunits of the main battery position and probably, but I can't be sure on this probably serviced by the gunners from the main positions so that would then cause, that would then cause the main position probably not to be able to fire, if they were firing from the other gun position, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were the guns in the sub-position, if I could call it that, of the same calibre as those in the main position, typically, or not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: In general terms, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever see gun batteries of different calibres? By that I mean, the battery of one calibre and then nearby a battery of a different calibre?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In some cases -- in some cases, the position would have up to three different calibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From your observations, were they all operated by the same gun crews or different gun crews, that is, the different calibres?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't -- I can't say exactly whether it would be from the same group. I suspect it would be, but I only would see one type being fired at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you form any opinion as to the degree of accuracy that the Serb gunners were capable of?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that opinion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: My opinion was that they were very --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: My opinion was that they were very -- very accurate in their firing in that the command post had the targets. The guns were well-maintained and the gunners were seem to be proficient on the weapons. Therefore, the accuracy should be -- should be fairly good, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In your military background, did you have any experience with any form of guns at all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I was a gunner initially in the reserves. I have also been qualified while in the infantry on mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you say you have been well-qualified in the infantry on mortar?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir on mortar and in Armoured [sic] Corps I was a troop leader and at a time as squadron commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How closely did you inspect the guns in the gun batteries on the Bosnian Serb army side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: My first time through in the positions that were not occupied by active gun crews, I went around and had a look at the mechanisms moved the barrels to check for play in the mechanism and had a look at the general maintenance and cleanliness of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you said the words "moved the barrels to check for play, I think you moved your arm up and down is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you detect any play in the barrels?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I am not an expert, sir, but there didn't see a lot of play at all. The mechanism seemed to be sound and tight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about the breaches?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The breaches, the breaches were well maintained. They were clean, rust free.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From your observations of the gun positions, did they move from time to time or did they tend to stay in the one place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Just stay in one place, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would that have any impact on their accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No. They would, if anything, allow any decrease in accuracy through movement and vibration on the mechanisms, that would be significantly reduced, which would allow the guns greater accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you able to -- I withdraw that. Is it the case that when operating artillery and mortars, typically there is a forward observation officer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And is that because often if not most of the time, the gunners cannot actually see the target they are trying to hit?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Bosnian Serb army had any forward observation officers in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know if they use forward observation officers at all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Not during the time I was there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean by that, that you don't know or that they didn't use them?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about sniping. In your movement around the Bosnian Serb army side of the confrontation lines, did you ever see any weapons which you were able to identify as being dedicated sniping rifles?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What brand of rifles were they?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I saw the weapons on a few occasions from a distance and they appeared to me to be drigonov.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that spelled d-r-a-g-o-n-o-v.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I think so, sir, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that a brand of a rifle?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is a sniper rifle, very effective. And easily identified by its configeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Specifically, what makes it easily identifiable?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: From a distance, the butt of the weapon is significantly different than any standard small arm that would be on the position and of course the telescopic scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How would you describe the length of the dragonov compared to other rifles?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Definitely longer, sir. Longer barrel [sic] and it is a much more sophisicated weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In your travels around the city, did you ever see people who appeared to be victims of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Firstly, did you ever see people who were dead, who appeared to victims of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I don't -- I saw people being carried away and in some cases it was obvious it was a wound and in other cases, it would be difficult to say. I would have to go and identify, which we did not do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever see individuals who were wounded apparently as a result of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever actually see anyone being shot in the city?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No. However, people were shot in areas that I was either at or had just arrived at, had been shot shortly before or out of my line of sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On those occasions where you arrived shortly after, did you ever see any individual who you concluded were without doubt, civilians?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about those individuals, that is, what it was about them which allowed you to conclude without did you tell that they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: In one specific case, sir, it was a young lad. He appeared to be about 12 or 13 years old and he had just passed my vehicle going around a wall and was brought back in about 15 seconds by two Ukrainian soldiers. He had been shot in the lower back.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you form any opinion as to the effect of the sniping of civilians and what you called the "random shelling" which occasioned civilian casualties on the population as a whole of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The areas that it was safe to move in for sniping, generally canalised the people away from the front lines and probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that word you said?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Canalised -- moved them from the front lines two or three blocks back from the confrontation line and then there would be barriers put up or whatever to allow them to go through crossroads so that then denied parts of the city for people and on the shelling in that it was random when you went out, you took your chances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were the barriers, that is the anti-sniping barriers effective?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: To a degree, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In what way were they not entirely effective?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: In some cases, the barriers were quite flimsy. In fact, in some cases there would be a series of blankets strewn across to -- basically to deny line of sight. In other cases, there would be gaps between containers that people would have to sprint across and as we were driving or walking, we also drove quickly or sprint.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why would you do this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Every position -- every location that afforded line of sight from the Serb side into the Muslim side was a potential place for a sniper to be. I know a little bit about sniping. So they would -- snipers would move their positions, sometimes not fire at all and other times fire on selected targets. That to say, if the individual, if the individual was a professional sniper, he would probably maybe fire one round and regardless of hit or miss, get out of there put his position to another street another window in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you notice any pattern to the sniping of civilians in Sarajevo from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Earlier I showed you a report for the month of January. I would like you to have a look at that again

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would be grateful if the witness can be shown Exhibit 752 and I note that is not a restricted document, that particular one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is it still on the desk of the witness, yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the transcript line -- page 45, line 8, it is recorded that when my colleague -- that my colleague and his side said Bosnian Serb, but I heard in the original the Bosnian side. This is pertaining to the sniping of civilians in Sarajevo. I believe that he said the Bosnian side, not the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation was Bosnian side, so it is not clear to me. Is it Bosnian side or Bosnian Serb side? It was at 16.41.47, the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I had a recollection that I said the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't remember. But is that how you understood the question, that you -- the question whether you saw any pattern in the-- let me just have a look. Any pattern to the sniping of civilians in Sarajevo from the Bosnian Serb side is that what you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer that you did not notice any pattern was related to Bosnian Serb sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that clarifies the issue, Ms. Pilipovic, then you may proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please turn to page 5 of the report and by consulting the bottom of page 4, does it appear that the first paragraph on page 5 refers to events which occurred on the 15th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the entry for that date, to think these words appear, "shelling of water queue in east Sarajevo killed and injured a large number of civilians," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Given the system of preparing these reports, are you able to say whether you would expect that event to have occurred on that date?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is hard for me, due to the speed, to follow what is being said. Could they please just tell us what date it was because this is page 5 of 13 and I believe they are working on the document -- on the report. P752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ierace was referring to page 5, but indicated that we would find the date on the last line of page 4, which is the 15th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now that clearly was a civilian target, I take it, a water queue in which a large number of civilians were killed and injured is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now you have spoken about random shelling. Apart from this particular incident did it come to your -- in the time that you were in Sarajevo, were you aware of other civilian targets being direct hits by shelling?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What type of civilian targets were direct hits?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Kosevo hospital to use the biggest example was targeted -- was targeted at a regular basis. The -- at times there would be targeting of to me obvious civilian areas, obvious civilian residential areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall any other civilian activities, apart from water lines that were targeted, apparently targeted?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The roadways. There was one funeral party that I wasn't there when it happened, but shortly after that was engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Of course, the roadway can carry military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were there any other lines of people, that is queues of people that were his apart from that particular one that you now remember during your three months in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There was one other. And that was a group of people standing just down from the PTT. They were waiting in a group for something. I am not sure what it was. And that group was targeted and they sustained casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you form any view as to whether incidents such as these were, first of all, as to where the shelling originated from, that is, which side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: In many cases, sir, that was exceptionally difficult for any number of reasons given, say like a wartime situation. But primarily and what bothered me the most was the mobility of the mortars to be able to get in, get a few rounds off, and get out of there before we could identify where they -- who had fired, where it was coming from and at times we had rounds landing on the city with no reports from the Serb side -- sorry, the UNMOs working on the Serb side, that they had fired. That they, the Serbs had fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you said that there were three -- I withdraw that. That there were 11 observation posts when you arrived on the Serb side is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you have observation posts at that stage that covered all of the Serb territory from which artillery or mortars could fire from and still hit targets in the city?
