utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Absolutely not, sir. That weapons could -- no, we did not. We could not cover the whole territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In other words, I take it, having regard to that answer, that the fact that there were no reports from UNMOs on the Serb side of a mortar or shell being fired, did not exclude the mortar or shell in question having originated on the Serb side, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It couldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence objects the question as phrased by my learned colleague. I believe this is more than just a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was careful to preface it with the words "having regard to that answer." In other words, I sought to clarify the implications of that answer and in my respectful submission, leading in that sense, is permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment to read again the questions carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has the opinion that Mr. Ierace is right in when he says that his question just expresses what is implicit in the answer of the witness. So please proceed, the objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Mr. Carswell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I do. It would be very difficult to say where that round have -- virtually impossible for any UNMO to say where that round came from. And we were careful not to make any kind of an indication on either point of origin or point of impact, if we were not exactly sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will take you back to page 5 of the monthly report. In the entry for the 16th of January, 1993 the third sentence reads "airport road closed for approximately 90 minutes this afternoon due to shelling and small arms fire and the airport was closed for 20 minutes due to what can only be regarded as deliberate sniper fire designed to kill as opposed to scare tactics." Now, do you recollect that particular activity on that day?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Not specifically that activity, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there activity, that is sniper activity, at the airport that you do recollect during your three months there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Most definitely, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that mostly in the daytime or the nighttime or equally both day and night?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It would drop by night, sporadic. However, by day depending -- depending on the whether any activities were being carried out by an aggressive manner by the Bosnian side. Sniping could go up to what I had indicated on the 16th where we would have to close off roads complete. Things were getting relatively serious at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At that stage, was there any movement of people across the runway of the nighttime?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I believe there was -- well, I know there was. The French Foreign Legion at that point were patrolling the runway and intercepting as best they could those who were crossing over land.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take you to the last sentence for that day which reads "more shelling close to the airport road and aimed sniper fire into the airport in addition to a continuation of people crossing the airport at night poses a major problem in this sector." Is that a correct reading of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does that refer to the crossing of the airport at night by people?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb military ever complain to you about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was their concern?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The airport had been given up by them to the UN to be used by and controlled by the UN. Their major complaint was that it should not or could not be used as any kind of a transit point for people in and of the city or to bring in any type of supplies or well basically any type of supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Amongst that traffic, do you know whether there were civilians?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I do not know. I didn't see it, but in my own mind, I am convinced that the majority of the traffic would be civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever make any observations of that human traffic at night?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Where did you make those observations from?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I was invited by the Serbs during one of my discussions over there to take a position overlooking the airport in one of the Serb infantry position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Mid-January.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You started off that the second last answer by saying, "I was invited by the Serbs during one of my discussions over there." Whereabouts did that discussion take place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I am not exactly sure, sir but I suspect it would have been Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect whether there was anyone any officers from Lukavica with you at the time you made those observations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There was one officer with me. He was an infantry from the position that I was observing from. He was not from Lukavica. He was from that particular position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was the -- I withdraw that. Was your attention drawn to an area of the runway or somewhere else in the airport complex?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Basically the runway, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was the runway lit at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you given any aids to assist your vision?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They gave me a night viewing device.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What type of night viewing device was it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It would have been a first generation image intensifier. What that does, is it uses the ambient light to magnify out to about 1.000 metres, 1.000 metres, possibly 1500.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What is the difference between an image intensifier and say a telescopic lens or lens which allows you to see infrared light?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: They're two different types of night viewing devises. Again, I am not a technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask you this: Does the -- did the image intensifier require a power source?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the power source?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I didn't specifically see it but it had a pack on the side that was -- what I am saying is I didn't specifically see the battery that it was enclosed. But it had a power pack -- it had what I assume to be a power pack on the side close to the on/off switch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Had you seen such a device before that night?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Not that particular type there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean by that, that you had seen image intensifiers before, but not that particular type?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: If you are talking about specifically Sarajevo area, no I had not seen any image intensifiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But you had seen them before in your life, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. I have used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, this particular image intensifier that you used on this night, did it appear to be designed for a particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It was much like the ones that we used a few years back. It could be mounted on a rifle, but that would be difficult in that it is very cumbersome on a rifle, probably more onto a lighter heavy machine-gun [sic]. Probably a heavy machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What is the weight of the image intensifier?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: At a guess, sir, and I am equating it to our own, probably about maximum 4 kilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What were the approximate dimensions, the one that you used that night?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It would be about a foot and a half long and much in general terms would look a bit like a light bulb in that the bottom end where the power was fed into the unit was simply to transmit the power from the battery pack and then the lens and the working parts were in a rather large cone-shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you looked through it, what was the nature of the image? Was it monochrome or colour?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It was first generation, sir. The colour comes out with a greenish tinge in it, so that would be the objects you would be looking at would be a very very slight greenish tint to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If there was any source of artificial light, say a hand held torch, let's say 500 metre, 800 metres how would that appear?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: That would appear as a light, a very definite light in using that source also to amplify the images, a very definite light in there, in the sight picture and that would additionally eliminate around the sight picture what was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Of course the torch is a directed beam. What about a candle light, that is a light which shed light rays in all directions. Would that have the same effect or different effect?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: A candle would probably be very much less, depending on distance, it would decrease over distance what you could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What on this particular night when you used it, what was the -- what were the sources of available light?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Star light and lights that were in and around the airport in that the French were patrolling with their Armoured Personnel Carriers so I could pick off their headlights.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you said you were looking at the runway area is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were the runway lights on or off?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Off.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: They were off?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it the nearest buildings would have been some distance from the runway?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: There was no light and no electricity at that point into Sarajevo and the separate power source at the airport was not used all that often to illuminate any buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to show the witness some further documents and I think we may have to do that in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we do it private session, Mr. Ierace, or could we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will try and avoid it. Perhaps see how I go?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you still have before you the monthly report, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first ask, Mr. Usher, I saw that there were some people in the public gallery. We have not turned in closed session and we might even not turn into closed session at all. It depends on whether it would be necessary, so I don't know whether they disappeared or not. But as far as I am concerned, this is in open session at this very moment, so would you please inform those who are there. You couldn't know, I am not blaming you for anything. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please go to page 8 of the monthly report. In particular, the entrance -- the entry for the 22nd of January 1993, the third sentence of the second paragraph reads, "The impacts have moved from seemingly indiscriminate shelling of the city to the areas of confrontation." Is that an accurate reading of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There seems to be a reference to impact of shells fired into the city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And is that indeed a reference to the type of indiscriminate or random shelling that you have described earlier?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The fire, if there are activities along the front line would obviously shift to the front line and the weight of the batteries, the weight of the guns would be brought to those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please go to page 10, in particular the entry for the 27th of January 1993 about halfway through that entry, do these words appear, "There was some shelling on the city which appeared to be random, however, the shelling along the front lines appeared to be concentrating in the areas of Rajlovac, followed by a grid reference Stup, followed by a grid reference, and Mojmilo, followed by a grid reference, all front line areas." Is that a correct reading -- an accurate reading of that passage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And does that refer to the type of random shelling of the city that you have spoken about earlier?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Initially, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And by "initially," do you mean the first part of that passage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might the witness be shown Exhibits -- two Exhibits to save time, P816 and P698.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Are these documents tendered under seal, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: They are, but Mr. President I am going to attempt to extract the evidence in a way which would not require us to go into private session. So at this stage I ask that they be shown to the witness and not placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I draw your attention to a point about two-thirds of the way down the first page.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Which Exhibit, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This is P816. I am sorry. And I ask you this question: In relation to the random shelling that you have described in your earlier testimony, did that affect, which parts of the city did that affect? In other words, which parts of the city received random firing from the Bosnian Serb army controlled side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: All sections, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During your time in Sarajevo, was there ever any negotiations -- withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it might be safe to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just make sure private session would duly protect the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am sorry. Given as I understand it, that private session involves no transmission of what is being said by the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- and counsel, that should suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20… [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 5.57 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic being in open session again, please proceed with cross-examination of Mr. Carswell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, we will remain with this document, it is a monthly report, P752. On page 4, under the entry January 15th when asked by my learned colleague you confirmed that you observed that there had been shelling of the water queue in the eastern part of Sarajevo and a large number of civilians had been injured or killed. So the entry of January 15th, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I don't have that, Madam Registrar. Page 4 of my 752, January 15th,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is page 4 and continues on page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When asked by my learned colleague you confirmed that this is what you had written down in your report is that true.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, as a member of the team of observers wasn't it mandatory for you when an accident of this nature took place, to visit the site of it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: As I indicated earlier, ma'am, not me specifically. One of the teams would have been dispatched there as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, can you please tell us which members of your team since you were the deputy of the high military observer, therefore, which member of your team visited this site following this incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Again, ma'am, I do not know. That would be in one of the patrol reports. The specific question, I can't answer that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you confirm for us that any observer visited the site following this incident and wrote a report for you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Judging by the way I have written the report, ma'am, one of my teams would have seen that if -- if any of the instances are not, using the term that we used at the time, "UNMO seen" it would be put down as local commander reports. My wording indicates that we had a team on the site at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Since you wrote down that this was in east Sarajevo and that a large number of civilians had been killed and injured, can you confirm to us that you had received a report and that based on this report compiled by your observers, you entered into the monthly report the text that I just read to you here, therefore, this item pertaining to east Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Allow me to read it again, please, ma'am. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us please when you say "east Sarajevo," can you tell us more precisely regarding this incident at what time exactly it took place, how many people were killed, and were you able to determine where the shells originated from?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I can't give you any of that detail. One of the -- to elaborate slightly. One of the problems that we had was that sometimes we would get a report such as this, which would cause us to dispatch a team down to the location and who in fact would arrive there after the fact. Now, I can't say specifically on this one whether that happened or not, but, again, judging from reading this, we would have had a team down there and they would probably have seen dead and injured, but some in all likelihood would have been moved away at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Since you are telling us that they probably saw dead and wounded, are you, in fact, saying that the observers who visited the site of the incident had an obligation to determine where the shells had originated from?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, sir -- no, ma'am. I am not saying that. The observers on the site would have absolutely no means to determine where that round came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you are telling us that the UN observers when visiting the sites of incidents and specifically this one never determined where the rounds had come from; is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, ma'am, that is not what I am telling you. In some cases, we would -- the observers that were on the positions, the gun positions on the Serb side that were firing, would be able to tell us when those batteries were firing, and it was a simple matter of judging time and space to understand in all likelihood where those rounds were landing. A second method to do it which was used over there but we didn't have that expertise with the observers was crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Specifically speaking about this instance, did you use one of these two methods that you just described for us?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I know I did not use crater analysis on that one. In that what we are looking at right now is an excerpt of my complete report and basically the high points of the day. I would have to look at my daily sit-rep for that day to identify whether anybody was able to report a round being fired or a number of rounds being fired from a certain location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So, therefore, you cannot confirm to us from which positions the water queue was shelled, nor can you tell in which part of the town this took place? You only know that it was in east Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: East on this report, ma'am, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Regarding this incident, when you were, therefore, unable to determine from which positions the water queue was shelled, you are, therefore, telling us that you did not inform either -- either warring side of this incident? When I say "either warring sides," by that I mean that you did not inform the army of Republika Srpska or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the UNPROFOR sector?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, ma'am, that is not what I am saying. I reiterate, this is an excerpt from my daily sit-rep which could very well have -- in fact would have paragraphs eliminated in that this simply were to be used in conjunction of the daily sit-rep, if somebody wanted to question that. And again, my daily sit-reps would probably be in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, you just told us about the entire daily report which gives in more detail what happened during the day. Can you please tell us, then, this daily report which had more details, who did you deliver it to and who did you forward it to when there are instances in which civilians were wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Every report, ma'am, regardless of the activity of the day, was delivered by approximately 2200 hours to the senior operations officer in the UNPROFOR headquarters, in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, on January 15th, who was high -- who was senior officer who was in charge of the analysis of this incident at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I don't know, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us whether these daily sit-reps which, as you say, were forwarded to the senior, to the high military observer did he then forward it on to somebody else? When I say "forward on" was it sent on to somebody within the warring -- sorry, was it sent on to somebody within the UNPROFOR structure or was it then forwarded it to one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, ma'am. The sit-rep had definitely not be forwarded to any of the warring parties. The information, as far as I know, was passed up to Zagreb and obviously copies would go to the commander in Sarajevo, and the actions would be taken from there. Now, I would also like to clarify one other point. When I told you I gave it only to the UNPROFOR headquarters, that is not entirely correct. I also passed on a copy to Kiseljak and a copy to UNMO headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us whether regarding this incident and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. following the receipt of information regarding this incident, whether you -- whether you informed the warring party within Sarajevo that there had been an incident in which civilians were wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Not that I would have used would have been to pass it through to our UNMOs in Lukavica who would in turn pass it on. And that would have done -- either have been done by radio or I would have gone over. I can't tell you which one -- which one I used, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell regarding January 16th when answering my learned colleague's question about the airport you spoke about shelling and shooting on the airport road. Can you tell us whether you were able to determine from which position they fired on the road and airport runway?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: For the artillery rounds I can't answer that question. I don't know. For the sniping and the firing that would cause the road to be closed again, this is not, understand, fresh in my mind. It probably would have been an action between the factions in that -- sorry, not the factions, the opposing sides, in that the road ran past the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you are telling us that the consequences of the shooting could have been the result of the combat that took place between the warring parties in the airport area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Not the shelling, ma'am. Definitely the small arms fire -- sorry. Definitely in all likelihood the small arms fire, that was fairly frequent occurrence. The small arms fire would probably have been an action between the opposing sides. The artillery fire or mortar fire would have been not tied up. The distance is too great.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The English transcript has missed the words, "strike definitely." That's an important omission because it effects the meaning significantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think proper care will be taken on that issue, but would we have to ask the perhaps the witness to repeat that part of the answer where he was using the words "strike definitely." Mr. Carswell, I have to explain to you that since hard work is done during the evening hours in the transcript and since we missed a small part, could you please then repeat your answer starting with "not the shelling that was an answer to the question whether the consequence of shooting could have been the result of combat. You said, "not the shelling, madam, definitely the small arms fire," and then please, the rest of your answer. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Strike definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, on January 16th, your entry on January 16th, line 9, which describes the events at the airport, you said that the general atmosphere was still tense. It is claimed by the Serbs that they will only fire in retaliation to Presidency force fire.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are referring to the 11th line, I suppose? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Therefore, you confirm for us that regarding these incidents which had taken place in the airport area, you talked about them to both sides? I am referring to this incident in the airport area.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Please allow me to reread this. That could have been me speaking or it could have been Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler speaking with them, ma'am. That was a statement I had heard a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, can you confirm for us that a large part of the airport runway was exposed to the front lines which were under the control of the BH army, if we look at the Dobrinja area and Butmir area, they were behind the airport and that area was under the control of the BH army, would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, in your monthly report on the entry on 21st of January, page 7, you write "that it seems that the military activity is switching to the nighttime when the small arms fire increases in town. It is very hard to make conclusions, however it is possible that this is a battle for power between Bosnian fractions within the town itself."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now when you describe these events on the 21st of January, when you described the struggle between Bosnian factions within the city, do you have any further knowledge which military formation this pertains to, if you meant military formations, when you said "Bosnian factions."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, ma'am. We had a lot of difficulty in that situations such as this to our knowledge -- too my knowledge, did not occur during the day. They could well have, but as I mentioned, not to my knowledge. However not regularly but occasionally at night, situations would occur of small arms fire in areas that we knew were definitely Bosnian controlled. Not on the confrontation line, but back from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On January 17th 1993 in your report you state the following on page 5, I am not going to read the entire entry, but here you speak about demonstrations and you say "that Serb women and children participated in demonstration asking that a large -- asking for a large scale of release of Bosnian held Serb POWs."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When compiling this report, did you have any specific information what POW's this refers to and where they were held?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: If we were given that information, ma'am, that would have been included in the patrol report and we, as UNMOs, didn't deal with POWs, but we would pass information when we were requested by either side. But that would go directly from us to the headquarters to pass to the relevant agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Carswell, in your monthly report in the January 24th entry on page 9, line 6 you said that "the Lima side UNMOs were called to the Blazuj hospital in order to witness that two of the oxygen bottles delivered by the UNHCR were found to contain gunpowder."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell can you tell us on whose side was the hospital in Blazuj, under whose control?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Unfortunately, ma'am I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If the Lima side UNMOs were called to the Blazuj hospital, could we agree that that was on the side that was controlled by the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It could very well be ma'am, but their mandate also stretched out in to some of the Bosnian areas that would be around there. Given the positioning of our UNMO locations, it was sometimes easiest for a team to be dispatched from the closest position, which could be up to 20 kilometres away, and that could cross over to a Bosnian position -- Bosnian held area excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, following the uncovering of the situation whereby UNPROFOR was transporting gunpowder in oxygen bottles, was there a special investigation following that and did you find out who these people were, UNPROFOR employees, who were transporting gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if it is a mistranslation. But the English transcript attributes UNPROFOR to my learned colleague as the transporter of the gunpowder. The passage that she read out refers instead to the UNHCR being the deliverer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But in my translation, it says that it was delivered by UNPROFOR. I am just reading what has been written, but if we are talking about UNHCR, then I would like -- I will ask Mr. Carswell whether UNHCR vehicles were escorted by UNPROFOR as security.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I can't speak specifically for this convoy but I expect there would have been -- there may have been an UNPROFOR escort, but I am afraid I don't know the composition of that particular convoy, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think that you didn't answer my question, whether following the delivery of gunpowder in oxygen bottles, you investigated within your service who was it that for the UNPROFOR knew that, that gunpowder was being transported in oxygen bottles, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Your question is not clear to me, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Following this incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was any investigation made in respect of this gunpowder?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Most definitely. That was not done by the UNMOs. Again we were the observers. That would be passed to headquarters, and then in turn passed on to whichever investigative agency would handle it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know that this would happen or do you assume that this is the way it would happen.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Having not seen the documents on the investigation, sir, it is an assumption based on what I heard in the headquarters of people discussing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, you told us that you heard that the headquarters, when people were discussing it, did you perhaps heard that this operation was called "operation oxygen" and that for quite a long period of time, this was done, that gunpowder was delivered in oxygen bottles?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, you told us that you arrived in Sarajevo on the 6th of January 1993 and that you stayed until the 20th of April 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Within those dates. I don't have my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, I apologise. I have my -- get my information from your statement. Can you confirm that on the 30th of June, 2000 you gave a statement to the investigators of the OTP in view of the circumstances of your stay in Sarajevo. So that was on the 30th of June 2000?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Like military even court have their own abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Carswell, the information that I would like information of comes from your statement that you arrived on the 6th of January and that you staid until the 20th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In your statement you said that in February 1993 there were 14 observation posts of military observers and asked by my learned colleague, you said that there were 11 observation posts on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I could well have said that. I didn't -- we -- on occasion, we moved our observation post depending on the circumstances. That was not particularly easy to do because we had to seek accommodation to do that. I can't remember specifically the locations of all the -- of all the OPs, the observation posts and their composition and my information I am taking from that -- those documents that I read in the past -- in the past few days when I talk about 11 OPs in 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But in any case, we can agree that there was a double number of observation posts on the Serb side compared the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you tell us perhaps whether you know, what was the criteria used to determine in the placement of these observation posts and why there was the double number of observation posts on the Serb side? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Obviously the line of confrontation that surrounded Sarajevo -- in fact encircled the city, the Serbs had both gun positions and forward infantry posts, we tried to site our OPs where we could best view what was going on. In some cases, it would be right where with the gun positions; in other cases, we would have them sited so they could hear the firing and identify which position it is coming from. I did not site those positions. They were in place when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that it would have been more efficient to have had more observers, observation points on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, we probably could have used about two or three more on the Muslim side, in that it was on the Bosnian side -- in that it was with three OPs difficult to cover the whole city, but not impossible. In that we sent out roaming patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you agree with me that it would have been more effective to have had more observation posts on the Muslim side, could we also agree that then you would have been able to establish on the side itself whether the army of Republika Srpska really fired on a location, would you then have been more precise?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Firing on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No. In real terms, ma'am, to properly monitor everything, you would virtually have to have a team of every position and every gun. As I mentioned earlier, with mobile mortars used by both organisations, the -- it was virtually impossible to cover all the ground. You simply can't do it, not with the numbers I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you confirm to us that because of difficult work and insufficient number of observers on both the Muslim side and the Serbian side, on the Serb side, you were not always able to establish with precision from which side the incident came or was caused in a certain part of town?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, in your statement on page 3 of the translation, that is the document 010060, I will formulate the questions in view of your -- in relation to your statement, you said that in the city of Sarajevo, there were about 10 Muslim brigades, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: If you -- that is what they were called, ma'am. To call it a brigade, though, in military terms is not correct. The numbers -- the numbers would vary in those organisations from 50 to maybe 250 so it was a brigade of soldiers as anywhere between about 3 and 5.000 in normal terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, I will show you a document, a Prosecution document, 0057561, which gives a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, have you taken proper care that no protected documents are used in such a way that the protection might become ineffective?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour I will first give my -- this document to my learned colleagues this is a Prosecution document, and if there is a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, and Mr. Ierace, may I just hear from you whether any specific measures are necessary at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then, please pass the document to the -- well, this is your copy, Mr. Ierace. Ms. Pilipovic, could you please provide a copy for the witness and copies for the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I tell you that this is a document which was compiled by Mr. Scott who was at the time also a member of UNPROFOR and that this is a list of brigades that comprised the first Corps, and on the first page you also have the report of the brigades of the Sarajevo -- on the second page you have the brigades of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. You can see on the second page the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you are now more or less summarising the content of the document. The witness told us that he doesn't know the document. Of course there is no problem in asking him anything about subjects dealt with in this document if he knows anything from his own knowledge about it, but we can't just confront him with the content of the document and then ask for comment and subsequently admit the document into evidence. So, I don't know what your plans are, but.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I will now ask a question that will not be in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, you said in your statement on page 3, when you were talking about the 10 brigades you said, "I travelled -- I tried to travel through their areas on a regular basis so that they would become familiar with me." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you tell us which were these brigades that comprised the 1st Corps of the BH army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand. Are you asking for the locations of their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will first ask you whether you know, considering that you visited the -- their areas, could you clarify, when you said "areas" what did you mean by that? What do you understand an "area" to be?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It would be an area of responsibility for an organisation within the overall -- the overall defensive position or the overall position. What I meant when I visited is that I tried to drive around there as often as possible. I did not specifically meet with the -- meet with the brigade commanders. I more drove the position so they got -- and I would encourage by UNMOs to do this -- so they were familiar with us. We did the same on the Serb side. We got to know them and they got to know us by face. And that makes it a lot easier to operate once the individuals know who you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell considering that you clarified what area of a brigade is, could you tell us in the Dobrinja area would you agree with me that in the Dobrinja area was the area of the 5th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically, ma'am, the positions of the units and their actual areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know, these brigades, were they positioned along the confrontation lines? Were they deployed along the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Deployed in a strict military sense, no. They would have soldiers forward and they generally the remainder of the unit would be back somewhat. It is not necessary in virtually any military operation to have all forward all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When we are talking about these 10 Muslim brigades, could you tell us whether -- do you know whether as part of these brigades, were also battalions, companies and detachments parts of these brigades?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, ma'am. That would -- I can't tell you that, but in my opinion, it would be impractical, given the numbers of people in the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the clarification for the transcript, your answer reads in the transcript "that would -- I can't tell you that, but in my opinion it would be impractical," which suggests that you could tell us. So not -- "I cannot" should be read as "I can tell you that." If you look at page 85, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: When she asked me sir, I was asked if I knew specifically how they were broken down, which I don't know. To elaborate on my answer, if a company-sized group requires a certain amount of command structure, if the particular brigade had maybe 200 total in it, that would be two companies in a normal rifle battalion. I am sure they did break down into smaller groups, but I wouldn't use those terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you could not tell us in full detail and it would be impractical as well, is that what you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, it would be impractical to break down like that, yes. THE COURT: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Carswell, if I tell you that in Sarajevo, the 102 Motorised Brigade at that time had 3.200 soldiers, would you agree that this is a correct information?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: No, I couldn't confirm that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell when we are talking about the brigade of the 1st Corps of the BH army, you said that you regularly visited these areas. Could you tell us when you visited these areas, where were the soldiers -- in what kind of facilities were they staying in, on these positions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I was never into any of their billets nor would I expect it to be in the context of a battle, that is privileged information. So I never did go to any of their billets. The reason I tell you they were not forward, is when something started to happen, you can see the soldiers coming in groups, twos and threes, forward to the battle, to join their unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you, when you toured the area of responsibility, did you also visit the command posts of the brigades that you toured and visited?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I did not visit all of the command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say that you didn't visit all of the places are you saying that you did visit some command posts? If you have, could you tell us which ones and which facilities were you at?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The two that I visited that are clear in my mind, ma'am, were in the south-east corner, in the south-east of the town of Sarajevo. To give you specific location I couldn't do that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you describe for us the buildings or the facilities where you were? Were these military facilities or were these residential buildings or were these apartments that were used by the army for their own purposes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: The two buildings were relatively close to each other, I would say within half a kilometre. One was beside a destroyed apartment -- sorry, destroyed -- it looked like a furniture store or clothing store. I wasn't sure what it was, but a commercial building. And the other one was in a warehouse district. Basically the offices of a warehouse were used in that one. Those were the only two that I can be relatively certain on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: These two buildings, these residential buildings where command posts of the brigades were, did they have any visible signs that you could see that these were military facilities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I would not use the term, ma'am, "residential." They were commercial, not residential and visible signs, definitely not would be advertising their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I tell you that so far in this case we have heard the testimony of many witnesses from the BH army areas, they said the soldiers were in private residential buildings, in schools, and in residential buildings that were on the front line; would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President to the representation of the evidence that is contained in that question on the grounds that it is not accurate. In particular, while there has been evidence that soldiers were in private residential buildings in the sense that they slept at home, and some further evidence in that regard, I don't recall evidence that they were in schools. I would be grateful if my friend could remind me of what that evidence was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will say that a witness who was not protected was heard here and he testified about the shelling of the water queue, Mr. Hussein Grebic, and who showed on a map of Sarajevo he pointed for Dobrinja, the command post for the 5th Motorised Brigade and on that occasion, I cannot be absolutely precise, whether which day it was, it was in Dobrinja; and he said they slept on abandoned buildings on the front line. And when I asked whether the school was working at the time, the witness said that the school was not working at the time because the army was staying there. I will check in relation to my question, but I will now withdraw it because I cannot be absolutely precise, if that is what you would like me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least, soldiers sleeping in a civilian building is perhaps not under all circumstances the same as having command post in civilian buildings. So I would not oppose against such a line of questioning, but with more detail. And if it can assist you to find that part of the evidence of Mr. Grebic, I would be glad to do so. So if you proceed, I will try to see whether I can find anything on that. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, in your statement when you said that you toured the areas of 10 Muslim brigades, could you tell us whether in that urban area of Sarajevo, according to you, could you tell us how large was that zone, that area of responsibility, including its length and depth, the area of responsibility of these 10 Muslim brigades?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Specifically, I cannot. It wasn't broken up evenly, I remember that. But I couldn't tell you whether it was 1.000 metres or 10.000 metres, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When touring these 10 Muslim brigades, were you able to determine what kind of weaponry they had?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: We had two means of doing that; obviously that which we saw while we were travelling, and then there was the heavy weapons collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which locations did your observers observe the artillery of the 1st Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: I am not -- I am not sure. Are you talking about weapons other than that at the collection points?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, did your observers follow the activity of the mortars that belonged to the 1st Corps and if they did, then from which locations did they do so?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Two methods to do that, ma'am. The first was -- I will back up a bit. As I mentioned earlier, they are mobile weapon, so those weapons would not be used from a static position over a period of time. So based on that, we didn't have any specific points to observe any mortar positions, however the first method was a -- hearing the mortar fire and that is somewhat difficult if there is other noises in the area. So mortar is not a loud weapon. And the second one was where we would observe something being towed, a weapon being towed. That was also difficult. The observation was not difficult. The observation was not difficult, but to follow that weapon, by the time we could get in our vehicles and get down there, they were gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In addition to mortars that we spoke about just now, did you have information that the 1st Corps of the BH army also had a Howitzer battery and then another Howitzer battery of 120 millimetres and also a battery of 122 millimetres that were within the 2nd 6th and 3rd, Motorised Brigade. I have in front of me a document in front of me dated 16 February 1993 from the 1st Corps, and therefore, I would like to know whether you, during your mandate, January, February, and March and April of 1993, were in a position to observe the activity of mortars and Howitzers that fired from the area that was under the control of the 1st Corps of the BH army, if not you yourself personally, then your observers?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: Whose document is that, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Carswell, this is a document belonging to the 1st Corps of the BH army, dated 16 February 1993. It is an order issued by the commander of the Corps and this is a document that was given to the Defence by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question that precedes this statement from my learned colleague really is two questions and an observation. And my learned colleague is now simply informing the witness of what she understands to be the origin of the document which really is of no assistance in cross-examination. The simple approach would perhaps be simply to ask the witness if he is aware of whether the ABiH had a Howitzer battery of 120 millimetres and so on, indicating that she is getting her information, that my learned colleague is getting her information from a particular document, this really doesn't assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked Mr. Carswell whether he had information that the 1st Corps of the BH army had Howitzer in their possession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say, "no ma'am," do you not know, or did you not have information?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL KENT CARSWELL
utterances.text: It was my impression at the time that there were no -- no weapons above the 120 millimetre mortars in the -- in the Bosnian positions within Sarajevo, other than those held -- those held at the collection points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, it is 7.00. I don't know whether this would be a suitable moment to break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication on how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to take less time than the examination-in-chief, so I believe that I will conclude within half an hour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am afraid, then, you are not taking less time, but more time. As far as my bookkeeping goes, the Prosecution took 1 hour and 30 minutes, and you are now up to 1 hour and 20 minutes. In order to give you, we started the examination-in-chief at a quarter past 3.00. We then until 10 minutes to 4.00. We started again at 16:25 and the examination-in-chief was finished by 10 minutes past 5.00. So that would make, if I am not making any mistake, even less than one hour and a half. I think you are approximately -- I am afraid I made a mistake in your favour already, if I said that you still had 10 minutes. But we will do the bookkeeping very carefully, Ms. Pilipovic, but I am afraid that you are further in time than you expected yourself. But in order to save time, it might assist you that when you refer to the testimony of Mr. Grebic, if you would look at Day 68, page 7295, at line 18, you will find a school with soldiers in it on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you give us an indication on well, whatever time Ms. Pilipovic would still take, how much time you would need for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So far I have only two questions until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Mr. Ierace, you promised us that you would check on whether the parts of the documents that were tendered or not tendered were -- we don't have to deal with it now -- but would you please inform us tomorrow so we can take a decision? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn until tomorrow at 2.15 p.m., same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th, day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
